newsitem.title: NORWAY: Germany seeks fair tax competition in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Germany seeks fair tax competition in Europe.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel called on Tuesday for a culture of fair tax competition to be established among countries in Europe.
"In the end, nobody has anything to gain from an unfair tax competition aimed at taking the tax from your neighbour," he said at the end of a two-day conference of 10 Baltic Sea border states.
"A tax competition with a dumping character will only hurt everyone," he told reporters.
European Union finance ministers have said they plan to harmonise tax policies, eliminate tax havens and reduce competition among member states aimed at luring investment.
"If we manage in Europe to obtain a culture of (economic) stability it must also be possible to obtain a culture of fair competition in the tax systems of Europe," he said.
Waigel mentioned no countries. But Germany's neighbour Luxembourg has become a tax haven for some Germans because it does not apply a withholding tax on interest.
Waigel was in the old Hanseatic town of Bergen on the Norwegian west coast to discuss economic cooperation with Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland.

Germany, impressed by economic growth rates in Nordic countries and the pace of reform in Poland and the three Baltic States, hopes a modern-day "Hanseatic league" in the region could attract EU regional funds and eventually rival the Mediterranean as an economic force
The Hanseatic League was a chain of cities that dominated trade in parts of northeastern Europe in medieval times.
"Closer cooperation is important to all of us," Waigel said.

The informal meeting followed a similar conference held a year ago in Boltenhagen, a German resort on the Baltic Sea, at Waigel's initiative. Next year, Sweden will host a third meeting of the 10 countries, only four of which are currently EU member states.

Waigel, who told the conference about preparations for European economic and monetary union (EMU), said the forum also provided a chance for some non-EU members to take part in the political discussion in Europe.

Norwegian Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg, who hosted the conference of finance ministers, said: "We had a very useful exchange of ideas on some of the most biggest economic challenges we are facing in northern Europe. We have seen we all face very much the same problems".
Norwegians in a referendum in 1994 voted against joining the EU. Iceland also has no plans to join, but Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland all want membership.
Denmark, an old EU member, has opted out of the EMU, due to start in 1999, following a 1993 referendum.

Sweden and Finland, both of which joined the EU in January 1995, have different approaches to EMU. The Swedes are undecided whether to join a single European currency but the Finns are officially in favour.
